candidates.title: Semantic Validation-Driven Iterative Refinement for LLM-Based Scientific Visualization
candidates.summary: This paper proposes integrating semantic validation of visual elements into LLM-based visualization agents to iteratively improve plot quality. The approach extends MatPlotAgent's visual feedback mechanism by adding structured semantic checks for data-plot consistency, addressing its limitation in detecting high-level visual-semantic mismatches. Evaluation uses MatPlotBench with metrics comparing output fidelity to human-verified ground truth, demonstrating improved accuracy over MatPlotAgent's native feedback system.
candidates.gap: MatPlotAgent (ref-001) detects low-level execution errors but lacks semantic validation of visual elements, failing to identify high-level mismatches between data and plot interpretations (e.g., incorrect axis scaling, misrepresented trends).
candidates.approach: Extend MatPlotAgent's feedback loop with a semantic validation module that (1) extracts visual features from generated plots, (2) compares them against expected data characteristics (e.g., trend direction, magnitude ranges), and (3) generates structured feedback for code regeneration. Uses GPT-4V for feature extraction and comparison, with feedback formatted as ["element_type", "expected_value", "actual_value", "severity"] tuples.
candidates.evaluation: Compare against MatPlotAgent baselines on MatPlotBench using (1) structural accuracy (axis labels, tick positions), (2) data fidelity (point deviation from ground truth), and (3) semantic correctness (trend/relationship mismatches). Measure improvement across refinement iterations with ablation study isolating semantic validation contribution.

candidates.title: Automated Process Supervision for Stepwise Verification in Mathematical Reasoning
candidates.summary: This paper introduces a method to train a reward model using automatically generated process-level feedback from program execution and symbolic validation. The model scores individual reasoning steps to enable targeted corrections during solution generation, improving accuracy on multi-step mathematical problems without manual annotations.
candidates.gap: While outcome-supervised value models (ref-015) and process-supervised models (ref-038) improve final accuracy, they either lack fine-grained step feedback (ref-015) or require manual annotations (ref-038). Ref-047 shows automated process supervision is possible but does not compare its step-level feedback quality against outcome-based baselines.
candidates.approach: Generate synthetic process-level annotations by executing reasoning steps as code and validating intermediate results symbolically. Train a reward model to score step correctness using these annotations. During inference, use the reward model to rerank solution paths by aggregating step scores, prioritizing paths with higher intermediate validity.
candidates.evaluation: Evaluate on GSM8K and MATH using (1) final-answer accuracy, (2) step-level error rate (proportion of incorrect steps in correct solutions), and (3) error propagation rate (proportion of solutions where an early step error invalidates the entire solution). Compare against outcome-supervised (ref-015), process-supervised (ref-038), and automated process-supervised (ref-047) baselines.

candidates.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning via Cost-Benefit Analysis for Multi-Agent Collaboration
candidates.summary: We introduce a method to dynamically prune redundant agents in multi-agent systems during task execution by evaluating their marginal contributions using a lightweight orchestrator. The approach combines task progress metrics with agent-specific performance indicators to identify non-essential agents for removal. Evaluated on ChatDev tasks, it achieves comparable performance to full systems at reduced computational cost.
candidates.gap: Existing dynamic multi-agent frameworks (ref-002, ref-042, ref-044) optimize agent coordination but lack explicit mechanisms to remove agents entirely based on their marginal contributions during task execution. Ref-002 prioritizes agents but doesn't eliminate them, ref-042 prunes messages but not agents, and ref-044 explores scaling but doesn't dynamically reduce agent counts.
candidates.approach: Implement a lightweight orchestrator that computes a cost-benefit score for each agent at discrete intervals using: (1) task progress metrics (percentage of subtasks completed), (2) agent-specific performance indicators (number of successful contributions vs. errors), and (3) computational cost (tokens consumed). Agents with negative marginal contribution (benefit < cost) are pruned. The orchestrator uses a threshold-based decision rule: if (current benefit / current cost) < (historical average benefit / historical average cost), the agent is removed. This differs from ref-002's prioritization and ref-042's message-level pruning by focusing on agent-level removal based on quantified marginal utility.
candidates.evaluation: Measure task success rate, computational cost (tokens used), and convergence speed (number of iterations to completion) on ChatDev software development tasks (ref-031). Compare against: (1) static multi-agent baseline (ref-031's full agent configuration), (2) ref-042's AgentPrune (message-level pruning), and (3) human-designed minimal configurations (5 experts selecting optimal agent subsets). Ablation study isolates pruning mechanism by comparing dynamic vs. static agent counts with identical agent implementations.
